The Tell-Atlas system is an EW stretching, ca. 2000 km long contractional belt that runs along the southern coast of Western Mediterranean Sea from Morocco to Tunisia. This belt is made of folds and thrusts generated by the continental collision between the Africa and Eurasia Plates. The thrust fault planes dip both to the north and to the south. This belt is thought to accommodate 4-5 mm/y of the total Africa-Europe convergence (Stich et al., 2006). A number of dextral strike-slip faults displace the folds and thrusts thereby creating a regional en-echelon pattern. This contractional belt is connected with the Apennineâ€“Maghrebide thrust system in western Sicily across the Sicily Channel, where submerged contraction features coexist with the extensional horst and graben pattern of the Pelagian Foreland (Corti et al., 2006; Fink et al., 2014).
Scarce information exists on the seismicity of this area. Historical and instrumental catalogs show some 4.5 < Mw < 5 events in western Sicily (SHEEC, Stucchi et al., 2012; EMEC, GrÃ¼nthal and WahlstrÃ¶m, 2012). The largest of these was that of 15 January 1968 (Mw 6.3).
This Source is a portion of the offshore southern (north-dipping) thrust front running from Hammamet (Tunisia) to the Sicily Channel. We constrained the strike of the source taking into account the geometry of the known fault traces and the orientation of geologic and geomorphic features (Corti et al., 2006; Fink et al., 2014). We inferred average dip and rake of this Source, along with slip rates, on the basis of regional tectonic and geodynamic considerations that took into account the characteristics of the whole contraction belt (EDSF, Basili et al., 2013). The maximum magnitude for this source was deduced from the 5 March 1823 earthquake, the largest event reported for this eastern portion of the contraction belt (Guidoboni et al., 2003; CPTI11, Rovida et al., 2011). This event is located off the northern coast of Sicily.
